title: 2026 budget confirmed with 6.4% tax increase
subtitle: Arts reserve fund, 2026 utility rates, Parkview Crematorium lease, pumping stations and a Weber Street North development.
overview: Council reaffirmed the 2026 budget with a combined property tax increase of 6.4%, unchanged from the original three-year plan {{vote:m17}}. Staff covered new pressures, including planning work moved from the Region, through net-zero adjustments. Council also used one-time reserve money to cover a shortfall in assessment growth, and added a planning manager and an assistant city solicitor.

Council set 2026 water, sanitary and stormwater rates, approved fee increases for rental housing, business licensing and building standards, and approved up to $11,000,000 for the Laurel Creek Sanitary Pumping Station. It ended municipal operation of the Parkview Crematorium on January 1, 2026 and approved a 10-year lease and equipment sale to a private operator. Prepaid cremation arrangements will be honoured by the new operator.

Council directed staff to create an Arts and Creative Industries Reserve Fund, with a policy due in June 2026 {{vote:m21}}. A competing amendment that asked for reports first was defeated {{vote:m20}}. Council also endorsed an official plan and zoning change for a grocery store at 200 Weber Street North, which still needs provincial approval.

decisions.detail: Council re-affirmed the 2026 operating budget with a 6.4% combined property tax increase (3.5% base and 2.9% service level and infrastructure), for a levy of $114,461,396 {{vote:m17}}.

decisions.item: Arts and Creative Industries Reserve Fund
decisions.detail: Council directed staff to establish the reserve fund, report back in June 2026 with a policy, and consider an initial contribution in the May 2026 year-end surplus report {{vote:m21}}.

Council set 2026 rates at $2.69/m3 for water and $3.11/m3 for sanitary, approved stormwater monthly charges, and approved a $125,000 increase to leaf collection and a $1,300,000 bulk water meter purchase.

Council ended municipal operation of the crematorium effective January 1, 2026, approved a 10-year building lease and equipment sale to Southwest Crematoriums Ltd., and stopped accepting prepaid services.

decisions.item: Laurel Creek and Conservation Drive pumping stations
decisions.detail: Council released $11,000,000 for the Laurel Creek Sanitary Pumping Station, directed staff to tender it, and approved in principle $11,400,000 for the Conservation Drive station from January 1, 2028.
Council endorsed Official Plan Amendment 63 and Zoning By-law Amendment Z-25-05 for a grocery store and directed staff to submit the flood-area package to the provincial ministries.
Council approved $823,000 of one-time funding from the Tax Rate Stabilization Reserve to cover the 2025 assessment growth shortfall.
Council approved a 12% increase to all Building Standards fees and charges effective January 1, 2026.

debate: On affordability, one councillor said residents consider the tax increase unaffordable and asked what was cut in response. Staff said the aim was to hold the previously approved rate, and that reaching about 5% would take roughly $1.5 million more in savings or deferred service increases, which staff had not modelled.

Staff said using more of the Tax Rate Stabilization Reserve would only defer the cost to the next term of council. They said fire expansion and sidewalk snow clearing are core service needs, not optional extras.

On the arts reserve, supporters said a dedicated fund would replace ad hoc funding, signal a long-term commitment and help the city match grants. Opponents wanted the culture plan, the large event strategy and comparison figures first. They also questioned opening a fund with no funding source, and asked whether the economic development reserve could be modified instead.

A staff member responsible for equity work said building equity consultation into the arts policy by June would likely be too short a timeline. Staff also said reserves have been established both before and after their policies, and that no money could be spent without council approval.

At the Weber Street North hearing, staff said the design does not appear to meet the Ontario Building Code because of safe exit concerns in a flood, so a building permit is unlikely. The applicant's planner said work with staff continues. A councillor noted this would be another grocery store in a flood-prone area, and another asked about noise, lighting and snow storage near neighbouring homes.
